speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The basis of my question took reference from a recent 18 March report published in the British newspaper, The Times.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With Speaker's permission, may I ask the Clerks to distribute copies so that Members can refer to it?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I have also informed the Minister for Law so that the article can be addressed in the Minister's response.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The article which the Member has distributed speaks of a "crisis in recruiting judges to the top levels of the bench" in the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It says that the UK courts are unable to attract high calibre legal talent to fill vacancies on the Bench.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One reason is said to be because of "a perception that   are not valued".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The article also says that the judges went to the Employment Tribunal to argue their case on their own remuneration packages, specifically pension arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the government is appealing against the Tribunal's ruling.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, here you have judges taking up their cases to the Employment Tribunal against the government; and now, the government is appealing against that decision.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think many of us would find this turn of events quite surprising.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The UK judiciary has always been perceived as being in an exalted position, highly valued, world-class and, really, beyond these sorts of squabbles.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our own legal system is derived from the British system, and we owe much to them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many of us grew up as lawyers, knowing and believing that the British judiciary was, in fact, the gold standard.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is, therefore, quite saddening to read this article.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of the difficulties faced by judges in the UK have been quite public for some time.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One of the reasons for this state of affairs, in my view, is that, for some time, the UK judiciary does not appear to have been given the resources it may have needed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And also, judges have been subjected to unfair public attacks.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These attacks have undermined the standing, prestige and morale of the judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2015, the then-Lord Chief Justice of the UK said that “there has, overall, been a widespread feeling   of not being valued or appreciated for their work”.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I referred Members to this when we discussed the Administration of Justice (Protection) Act (AOJP Act).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This state of judicial morale in the UK owes somewhat to the attacks on judges by the British media.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You can imagine that the standing of the judiciary in the eyes of the public does not get enhanced when these sorts of attacks are made by mass circulation media.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In an earlier 2014 UK Judicial Attitude Survey, almost two-thirds or 62% of all judges said that members of the judiciary are respected by society less than they were 10 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Half of all judges – in fact, more than half – 56% of all judges saw media representation of judges and 59% saw public misunderstanding of the judiciary as factors which drove these changes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I also referred Members to this during the AOJP debate.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not difficult to see why when you have newspaper headlines labelling judges as "Enemies of the people" and "You fools" when the courts decide in ways that the media dislikes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Internet, social media in particular, seems to have worsened the problem.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The current Lord Chief Justice, in a press conference in December last year, said that judges are facing "an increasing torrent of personal abuse online", some of which was designed to intimidate them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the 2016 Judicial Attitude Survey I earlier cited, 15% of the respondents – the judges – said they had concerns about their own personal safety on social media.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The situation we have in Singapore is slightly different.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In fact, if you see these sorts of surveys across the system – I am particularly aware of the Police, the Courts and the legal system – they all have about 90% or above in terms of trust.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A State Courts user survey that same year found that 95% of users of our Courts had confidence in the fair and effective administration of justice by the State Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But this is not cast in stone, and what is happening in the UK could easily have happened in Singapore and can easily happen to us if we are not careful.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The reason it has not happened is because we have chosen a different path from the UK in some ways.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, there is a considerable difference between the UK and Singapore in our respective approaches to the remuneration of judges.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think the article says that a Senior Judge could get about £181,000, which equates to something slightly less than S$400,000 today.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For us – the records are public – top practitioners do take a pay cut when they become Judges and, depending on where they were outside, it could be a significant pay cut.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some could take as much as a 70% to 80% pay cut.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But many others might take a 10% to 20% pay cut.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But in the UK, if you take a top silk earning ₤2 million or more, then you will see the difference on average.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the cut that our judges take is there, but it is not as steep as in many other countries, including the UK.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We also seek to appoint the best people from the private and public sectors to the Bench and key Legal Service appointments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our Chief Justice himself was a leading practitioner who was highly regarded both in Singapore and on the international stage.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Before he went on to the Bench, he was Attorney-General and then he went on to head the Judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is important, and we have to make sure that it remains such that, while there is a cut, it cannot come to a stage where judges feel that they are paid so little that they do not want to take it up, which is the situation seen in many places.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or you certainly do not want them going to Employment Tribunals, and appealing and arguing about their own remuneration.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, we have been clear about protecting our Judiciary from abuse and contempt.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When we passed the AOJP Act in 2016, there were suggestions that we ought to, in fact, abolish the offence of scandalising the Judiciary, as the UK has done.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The UK Law Commission did recommend the abolition of the offence, but it noted that "there   a great deal of extremely abusive online material concerning judges".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It also observed that the UK Judiciary had lost the deferential respect it used to enjoy and lamented that "this change is one to be regretted", and since the situation was so bad and all the judges were being attacked online, and because the UK judiciary no longer had the deferential respect, there was little point in keeping the offence because you cannot reverse it anyway.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The offence of scandalising the judiciary was, therefore, of limited value in the UK, because scandalising the courts was very common.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Questions were asked then, in the House as well as outside: "Other countries are going in the opposite direction.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Why do we not follow them?" My answer is a simple one – we follow other countries if it makes sense, and we frequently look at the practice of other countries and more mature societies – what is good, what will work, we are happy to take.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But when it makes sense, we must also be confident in charting our own paths.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is important that we are not colonised in our minds.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the test – since the AOJP has become law, has freedom of speech suffered?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Have legitimate, free discussions on Court cases been stifled?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we were to compromise on this, the effects will not be felt this year, next year or in the next two years.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But some years later, we are likely to find ourselves in the same position that the British find themselves today – judges feeling under attack or judges being under attack; distrust generally pervading; and an inability to attract top legal minds to take up positions on the Bench.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When the quality of the Judiciary suffers, the rule of law suffers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When the rule of law suffers, the country suffers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: My questions are: one, how do we keep the public's esteem for our Singapore Judiciary at a high and a continued high such that it is important to maintain our rule of law standing as a country?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The same goes for many other parts of the Public Service, including political officeholders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regards the Member's first question as to how we keep the enhanced standing of our Judiciary intact, I would, in fact, go further.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we have a unique window of opportunity to make sure that our Judiciary is not just respected within Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the development of Asia today – the huge economic growth – and the fact that if you look around in Asia, which place really stands out as the one place that has outstanding rule of law, outstanding judges, lawyers and where you can get your legal business done properly?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think there are only two places that will seek to claim that position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One is Hong Kong and the other is Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not an unbiased party in this, but I believe that we are ahead.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not only that, but I believe that we are putting clear blue water between ourselves and Hong Kong, in that respect, for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You get world-class judges sitting there hearing cases, and it can be in any law, and it may have no connection to Singapore and Singapore is a forum that they trust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we should not only maintain the standing of the Judiciary which, as I have said earlier, is not a given, but we have to work hard at it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that means continuing to get the best available legal talent, make sure that the standing of the judiciary is not subject to unfair attacks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their judgments can be subjected to any sort of criticism you want as a matter of law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can say they have gotten their law wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can say that you disagree with them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you believe there are improper reasons, the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB) will investigate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No one, in that sense, is above the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we need to make sure of that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you need a Government that is strong enough to make sure that it protects the standing of the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We had a verdict in the City Harvest case in the Court of Appeal in February.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In terms of the actual sentences that were imposed, it is quite clear that the Government took the view that the sentences were not adequate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We had said it even before the Court of Appeal ruled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We had said the sentence was not adequate, which was why the Public Prosecutor appealed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was also clear that substantial public sentiment was very much not in favour of the judgment that was delivered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, politically, the easiest thing – and that happens in many places – would have been for the Government to come to Parliament if it wanted to make a point and also join in, in the criticism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is most unlikely that you will get a situation where the Minister for Law will stand here and say, while we disagree with the final result, nevertheless, judges ought not to be attacked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They ought to be respected, supported and be given the freedom to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we disagree, we criticise their judgments, but let us not criticise them personally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need a Government – and I hope this is common to all Members here, and I believe it is common to all Members here, both Government and Opposition – that is very strong in protecting the standing of our Judiciary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thankfully, we have not had debates in this House, nor among reasonable opinion outside, about the Judiciary along the lines that are taking place in many other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thankfully, we do not have that and, therefore, we are able to deal with the substantive issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One can argue, agree or disagree on specific aspects of the AOJP, but I do not think there is disagreement on the fact that our Judiciary has to be protected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I checked it, but I will check that again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if I have to correct it, I will come back and let the Member know.
